Frontiers in Pharmacology frontiersin.org 01 GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT 1 Introduction Within the landscape of emerging infectious diseases, there are pathogens that, despite remaining far from the spotlight for long periods, continue to represent a constant source of uncertainty for global public health. Some of them emerge suddenly, spreading rapidly and placing considerable pressure on healthcare systems, economies, and societies worldwide. Others, however, follow a more discreet path: they persist silently within natural ecosystems, causing sporadic human infections and attracting only limited attention until an unexpected outbreak or a series of unusual epidemiological events brings their potential threat back to the attention of the scientific community and the media. Hantaviruses belong to this latter category. Despite the relative rarity of human infections, these zoonotic pathogens continue to raise questions regarding their true public health impact and the risk they may pose in the context of future infectious disease emergencies (Kumar and John, 2026). Nevertheless, despite substantial advances in hantavirus research, important knowledge gaps remain regarding their future epidemiological impact, the ecological drivers of spillover, and the development of effective therapeutic strategies. Behind the relatively small number of human cases lies a biologically complex family of viruses. Hantaviruses belong to the family Hantaviridae, within the order Bunyavirales, and are enveloped viruses with a spherical morphology measuring approximately 80–120 nm in diameter. Their genome consists of a negative-sense single-stranded RNA segmented into three fragments, designated Small (S), Medium (M), and Large (L). The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (N), which is involved in encapsidation of the viral genome; the M segment encodes the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc, which are essential for host cell entry; whereas the L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), responsible for viral transcription and genome replication (Bradfute et al., 2024; Vaheri et al., 2013). Replication occurs entirely within the cytoplasm of the infected cell. Following the binding of the viral glycoproteins to host cell receptors, the virus enters the cell by receptor-mediated endocytosis. After acidification of the endosome, the ribonucleocapsids are released into the cytoplasm, where the viral RNA polymerase initiates the synthesis of messenger RNAs and new genomic copies. Assembly of mature virions occurs predominantly within the Golgi apparatus, from which newly formed viral particles are subsequently released (Vaheri et al., 2013; Vial et al., 2023). The apparent genomic simplicity of hantaviruses should not be misleading. Like many RNA viruses, they possess remarkable evolutionary plasticity, largely due to the lack of efficient proofreading mechanisms during genome replication. The progressive accumulation of mutations, reassortment between different genomic segments, and adaptation to novel reservoir hosts have contributed over time to the considerable genetic Frontiers in Pharmacology frontiersin.org 02 Di Maria and Provenzani 10.3389/fphar.2026.1925640 diversity observed within the Hantaviridae family. Although most of these genetic changes do not necessarily translate into increased transmissibility or virulence, the continuous evolution of hantaviruses remains one of the main factors driving scientific interest in these pathogens and their emerging potential (Vial et al., 2023; Klempa, 2018). The history of infectious diseases has repeatedly demonstrated that many epidemics and pandemics have originated from spillover events, namely, the transmission of pathogens from their animal reservoirs to humans. One emblematic example is plague caused by Yersinia pestis, the agent responsible for the Black Death in the 14th century and for the subsequent epidemic that struck the Duchy of Milan between 1629 and 1631, famously described by Alessandro Manzoni in The Betrothed (Plo et al., 2017). Likewise, hantaviruses represent a paradigmatic example of an emerging zoonosis. Their natural reservoirs consist predominantly of wild rodents, which harbor the virus persistently and generally remain asymptomatic. Human infection occurs accidently through the inhalation of aerosols contaminated with infected urine, saliva, or feces, without the need for direct contact with the animal (Tortosa et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2017). The public health risk associated with hantaviruses therefore stems not primarily from their ability to sustain human-to-human transmission chains, but rather from the continuous exposure of humans to ecosystems in which the virus naturally circulates. Climate change, habitat fragmentation, deforestation, and the expansion of human activities into rural and peri-urban environments are progressively increasing opportunities for contact between humans and wildlife, thereby creating favorable conditions for new spillover events and the emergence of unexpected outbreaks (Fabbri et al., 2025). Recent evidence has further highlighted how climate change, biodiversity loss, and land-use modifications are reshaping pathogen ecology and increasing opportunities for zoonotic spillover, reinforcing concerns regarding the future emergence of hantavirus outbreaks and other emerging zoonoses (Carlson et al., 2025). As a consequence, a genuine environmental pressure is reshaping human exposure to these pathogens through changing ecosystem dynamics. However, unlike highly transmissible respiratory viruses, hantaviruses generally do not sustain human-to-human transmission (Toledo et al., 2022). Within the biological and virological diversity of hantaviruses (Hepojoki et al., 2015), Andes virus (ANDV) represents a notable epidemiological exception, as person-to-person transmission has been documented under specific conditions, particularly following close and prolonged contact (World Health Organization, 2026a). Epidemiological and virological studies from South America have documented transmission within households and healthcare settings and characterized viral shedding during acute infection (Martinez-Valdebenito et al., 2014; Ferrés et al., 2024). A recent systematic evidence assessment further indicated that documented person-to-person transmission is restricted to ANDV, with no evidence of asymptomatic or presymptomatic transmission (UK Health Security Agency, 2026). Although transmission clusters and occasional superspreading events have been reported under specific circumstances (Martínez et al., 2020), the available evidence does not support sustained transmission within the general population. Beyond the unresolved epidemiological questions, major uncertainties also persist regarding the therapeutic management of hantavirus infection. Clinical care remains largely supportive, while no antiviral therapy has yet demonstrated consistent clinical benefit in adequately powered randomized trials. Recent advances in antiviral discovery, including computational drug design, natural product-based approaches, targeted drug delivery, and host-directed therapeutic strategies, have renewed interest in the development of novel interventions for hantavirus infection. Accordingly, investigational approaches including direct-acting antivirals, broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, immune-based interventions, and host-directed therapies have shown encouraging activity in experimental models and early clinical studies; however, no pharmacological intervention has yet demonstrated unequivocal efficacy in randomized clinical trials, and the available evidence remains fragmented. These gaps underscore the need for well-designed clinical trials to establish the safety and efficacy of emerging antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and host-directed therapeutic strategies, which remain key priorities for future research (Martin and Tripp, 2024; Afzal et al., 2023; Lanrewaju et al., 2026). So, is hantavirus merely a flash in the pan, or an emerging threat? The currently available evidence suggests that the answer depends less on the limited human-to-human transmission observed today than on the ability of these viruses to persist within their natural reservoirs, adapt to ecological changes, and continuously generate new opportunities for spillover (Provenzani and Polidori, 2020). From this perspective, hantaviruses do not represent an imminent pandemic threat; rather, they constitute a paradigmatic example of a persistent zoonotic risk that requires continuous epidemiological surveillance, clinical preparedness, and an integrated One Health approach. Although previous reviews have comprehensively summarized hantavirus biology, epidemiology, and clinical manifestations, recent advances in therapeutic research warrant an updated critical appraisal of emerging pharmacological strategies. Accordingly, this review integrates current evidence on antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, immune-based interventions, and host-directed therapies while highlighting the principal unmet clinical needs and priorities for future research. 2 Methods This work was conducted as a narrative, non-systematic review aimed at providing an updated overview of the epidemiology, clinical management, emerging therapeutic strategies, and public health implications of hantavirus infections. A comprehensive literature search was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE as the primary biomedical database. Searches combined free-text terms and, where appropriate, Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) using Boolean operators (AND, OR). Search terms included “hantavirus”, “hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome”, “hantavirus pulmonary syndrome”, “Andes virus”, “Seoul virus”, “kidney transplantation”, and “companion animals”. Additional searches were conducted in ClinicalTrials.gov to identify ongoing and completed clinical trials related to hantavirus therapeutics and vaccines. Frontiers in Pharmacology frontiersin.org 03 Di Maria and Provenzani 10.3389/fphar.2026.1925640 To incorporate the most recent epidemiological evidence and international public health recommendations, additional information was retrieved from authoritative institutional sources, including the World Health Organization (WHO), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), and the Istituto Superiore di Sanità (ISS). Particular attention was devoted to the WHO Disease Outbreak News reports, the Hantavirus Outbreak Toolbox, and the interim guidance documents published following the 2026 Andes virus outbreak associated with the MV Hondius expedition. The literature search covered publications from database inception through June 2026. Eligible sources included narrative and systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, observational studies, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case reports, case series, clinical practice guidance, outbreak investigation reports, and official documents issued by international public health agencies. Reference lists of the selected publications were also manually screened to identify additional relevant studies. Evidence was critically appraised and synthesized to provide a balanced overview of the current knowledge regarding hantavirus epidemiology, zoonotic transmission, pharmacological management, emerging therapeutic approaches, infections in immunocompromised and solid organ transplant recipients, and the implications of recent international outbreaks. Owing to the narrative design of this review, no quantitative synthesis or meta- analysis was performed. TABLE 1 One health perspective on hantavirus transmission. Some of them emerge suddenly, spreading rapidly and placing considerable pressure on healthcare systems, economies, and societies worldwide. Others, however, follow a more discreet path: they persist silently within natural ecosystems, causing sporadic human infections and attracting only limited attention until an unexpected outbreak or a series of unusual epidemiological events brings their potential threat back to the attention of the scientific community and the media. Hantaviruses belong to this latter category. Despite the relative rarity of human infections, these zoonotic pathogens continue to raise questions regarding their true public health impact and the risk they may pose in the context of future infectious disease emergencies (Kumar and John, 2026). Nevertheless, despite substantial advances in hantavirus research, important knowledge gaps remain regarding their future epidemiological impact, the ecological drivers of spillover, and the development of effective therapeutic strategies. Behind the relatively small number of human cases lies a biologically complex family of viruses. Hantaviruses belong to the family Hantaviridae, within the order Bunyavirales, and are enveloped viruses with a spherical morphology measuring approximately 80–120 nm in diameter. Their genome consists of a negative-sense single-stranded RNA segmented into three fragments, designated Small (S), Medium (M), and Large (L). The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (N), which is involved in encapsidation of the viral genome; the M segment encodes the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc, which are essential for host cell entry; whereas the L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), responsible for viral transcription and genome replication (Bradfute et al., 2024; Vaheri et al., 2013). Replication occurs entirely within the cytoplasm of the infected cell. Following the binding of the viral glycoproteins to host cell receptors, the virus enters the cell by receptor-mediated endocytosis. After acidification of the endosome, the ribonucleocapsids are released into the cytoplasm, where the viral RNA polymerase initiates the synthesis of messenger RNAs and new genomic copies. Assembly of mature virions occurs predominantly within the Golgi apparatus, from which newly formed viral particles are subsequently released (Vaheri et al., 2013; Vial et al., 2023). The apparent genomic simplicity of hantaviruses should not be misleading. Like many RNA viruses, they possess remarkable evolutionary plasticity, largely due to the lack of efficient proofreading mechanisms during genome replication. The history of infectious diseases has repeatedly demonstrated that many epidemics and pandemics have originated from spillover events, namely, the transmission of pathogens from their animal reservoirs to humans. analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonotic viruses that continue to pose a public‑health concern despite their relatively low incidence in humans. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on recent epidemiology, the 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship outbreak, the role of companion animals, infections in solid‑organ transplant recipients, and emerging therapeutic strategies. (A3)
analysis.current_state: Supportive care remains the standard; ribavirin shows limited benefit only when given early in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, while neutralizing monoclonal antibodies and host‑directed therapies are promising in pre‑clinical studies but lack robust clinical validation. Companion animals are not natural reservoirs but may serve as sentinels of local hantavirus circulation. (A5, A6, A7)
analysis.gaps: Key uncertainties include transmission dynamics and vulnerable populations highlighted by the 2026 outbreak, the paucity of clinical data for new immunotherapies, and diagnostic challenges in immunocompromised patients where infection can mimic graft rejection. (A2, A7, A8)
analysis.future_research: Priorities are integrated One‑Health surveillance, rapid diagnostic development, and controlled clinical trials of neutralizing antibodies and host‑targeted drugs, together with studies on pet‑rat‑associated Seoul orthohantavirus spillover and the sentinel value of companion‑animal exposure. (A9, A11)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonoses that, despite low human incidence, remain a persistent public‑health concern. Main directions: The review examines recent epidemiology, the 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship outbreak, the role of companion animals, infections in solid‑organ transplant recipients, and emerging therapeutic strategies. Current state: Supportive care is still the mainstay; ribavirin shows limited benefit early in HFRS, while pre‑clinical monoclonal antibodies and host‑directed therapies appear promising but lack clinical validation, and companion animals are not natural reservoirs but sentinel indicators. Gaps: Key uncertainties include transmission dynamics and vulnerable groups highlighted by the 2026 outbreak, the paucity of clinical data for new immunotherapies, and diagnostic challenges in immunocompromised patients. Future research: Priorities are integrated One‑Health surveillance, rapid diagnostic development, and controlled trials of neutralizing antibodies and host‑targeted drugs, plus studies on pet‑rat‑associated Seoul virus spillover.

papers.title: Hantaan virus polymerase has an in vitro Terminal Nucleotidyl Transferase activity that is conserved across the Bunyaviricetes class
papers.abstract: Bunyaviricetes is a class of segmented negative strand RNA viruses (sNSV) that includes causative agents of severe zoonotic diseases resulting in hemorrhagic fever in humans and livestock. Hantaan virus (HTNV), family Hantaviridae, is an example of life-threatening bunyavirus transmitted by rodents which leads to Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans. Infection relies on the replication and transcription of their tripartite genomes through multifunctional RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) in the context of ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) made of one viral RNA fragment, one RdRp and multiple copies of viral nucleoproteins. The RdRp, also known as L protein, performs replication by de novo initiation through a prime-and-realign mechanism while transcription initiates through a cap snatching mechanism, that engages a cap-binding domain and an endonuclease (EN) domain present in the L protein C and N terminal regions, respectively. In this work we show that HTNV L protein has a terminal nucleotidyl transferase (TNTase) activity over double-stranded RNA substrates (dsRNA) in vitro. We show that the TNTase activity is also present in other bunyaviral L proteins by comparing HTNV L protein activity with La Crosse (LACV, family Orthobunyaviridae) and Crimean Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV, family Nairoviridae) L proteins. Our results show that TNTase activity appears to be a general feature of Bunyaviruses and report the differences on substrate and nucleotide specificity for each family of virus.

analysis.background: Bunyaviricetes are a class of segmented negative‑strand RNA viruses that include agents causing severe zoonotic hemorrhagic fevers; Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent‑borne hantavirus that causes HFRS in humans.
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: HTNV L protein shows terminal nucleotidyl transferase (TNTase) activity on double‑stranded RNA in vitro; comparable TNTase activity is detected in L proteins of La Crosse virus and Crimean‑Congo hemorrhagic fever virus, indicating the activity is conserved across families, with each family displaying distinct substrate and nucleotide preferences.
analysis.contribution: The study identifies TNTase activity as a general feature of Bunyaviricetes, advancing understanding of viral replication mechanisms and suggesting a potential broad‑spectrum antiviral target.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; experimental details, quantitative measurements, and in‑vivo relevance are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Bunyaviricetes are segmented negative‑strand RNA viruses causing severe zoonoses; Hantaan virus causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: HTNV L protein exhibits terminal nucleotidyl transferase activity on dsRNA in vitro, and similar activity is present in La Crosse and Crimean‑Congo hemorrhagic fever virus L proteins, indicating conservation across families with differing substrate and nucleotide specificities. Contribution: Reveals TNTase activity as a general Bunyaviricetes feature, informing replication biology and potential antiviral strategies. Limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed methods, quantitative data, and in‑vivo relevance are absent.

papers.title: Climate change, rodent ecology, and the rising risk of hantavirus outbreaks: an alarming public health concern
papers.abstract: The Anthropocene era has been characterized by a higher risk of zoonotic viral outbreaks, which often result from a combination of factors, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, land-use patterns, and increased opportunities for human–animal interactions. The current perspective provides an integrated synthesis of how climate change-driven alterations in rodent ecology impact the molecular evolution, transmission dynamics, and emergence of hantaviruses, with an emphasis on the underlying virological mechanisms and their implications for One Health preparedness. Hantaviruses have undergone extensive diversification throughout their evolution and host adaptation and can infect rodents, bats, reptiles, and fish. Rodents serve as the principal natural reservoirs for hantaviruses, with many viral species exhibiting long-term evolutionary associations with specific rodent host species. Climate change has been recognized as one of the key determinants for the emergence of hantavirus outbreaks in different parts of the world. Climate-related factors may facilitate viral amplification through multiple mechanisms, including their impact on evolution, mutation, and reassortment. To conclude, climate change has shaped the ecology, transmission dynamics, and molecular evolution of hantaviruses by altering rodent behavior, their habitats, and the environmental persistence of viral particles. Climate-induced ecological disruption has created opportunities for viral amplification within reservoir hosts and augmented the risk of zoonotic spillover into humans. These insights provide a conceptual framework for anticipating future outbreaks in the context of climate change and support the integration of ecological, virological, and public health surveillance systems. There is an urgent need to ensure that virological preparedness strategies evolve in accordance with changing environmental conditions by strengthening genomic surveillance and integrated One Health frameworks.

Rodents serve as the principal natural reservoirs for hantaviruses, with many viral species exhibiting long-term evolutionary asso­ ciations with specific rodent host species. Climate change has been recognized as one of the key determinants for the emergence of hantavirus outbreaks in dif­ ferent parts of the world. Climate-related factors may facilitate viral amplification through multiple mechanisms, including their impact on evolution, mutation, and reassortment. KEYWORDS climate change, climate-sensitive infectious diseases, hantavirus, one health, rodent ecology, viral evolution, zoonotic spillover Shrivastava et al.  10.3389/fmicb.2026.1943856 Frontiers in Microbiology 02 frontiersin.org 1 Introduction In the current Anthropocene era, an unprecedented rise in the risk of zoonotic viral outbreaks and epidemics has been reported, often driven by climate change, biodiversity loss, human activities that alter the natural landscape, and increased opportunities for human– animal interactions (Plowright et al., 2021; Sánchez et al., 2021). A rise in the probability of the emergence of infectious diseases with epi­ demic or pandemic potential has been reported in the last few decades due to environmental disruption, which has increased spillover from wildlife reservoirs to human populations (Plowright et al., 2021). With increasing climate-sensitive viral outbreaks, there is a crucial need to understand the ecological determinants of virus transmission and the necessity to adopt integrated One Health surveillance frameworks (Stephens et al., 2021). In fact, artificial intelligence-based predictive models have estimated that climate-induced shifts in wildlife distribu­ tion can facilitate novel cross-species viral transmission in the future (Grange et al., 2021). Among zoonotic pathogens, hantaviruses have attracted signifi­ cant scientific attention because they are highly adaptable rodent- borne RNA viruses capable of causing severe diseases, namely, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmo­ nary syndrome, in humans (Munir et al., 2021). Moreover, changing climatic conditions, such as varying rainfall patterns, warmer tem­ peratures, and ecological instability, can influence fluctuations in res­ ervoir populations of rodents and create more opportunities for hantavirus transmission to humans (Vial et al., 2023). Recent studies and developments have improved our understanding of the ecology of the causative viruses, environmental determinants, and surveillance approaches (Munir et al., 2021; Ramos-Nino et al., 2026; Vial et al., 2023). However, the majority of studies have focused on exploring climate variability, rodent population dynamics, viral evolution, and public health preparedness as separate domains (Fabbri et al., 2025; Grange et al., 2021; Munir et al., 2021; Ramos-Nino et al., 2026; Stephens et al., 2021; Vial et al., 2023). The current perspective pro­ vides an integrated synthesis of how climate change-driven alterations in rodent ecology impact the molecular evolution, transmission dynamics, and emergence of hantaviruses, highlighting the underlying virological mechanisms and their implications for One Health preparedness. 2 Hantaviruses: virological and molecular overview Hantaviruses belong to the family Hantaviridae (order Bunyavirales), which includes multiple genera and several species, the majority of which are pathogenic to humans (Kuhn and Schmaljohn, 2023). These viruses have shown extensive diversification in their evo­ lution and host adaptation as they can infect rodents, bats, reptiles, and fish (Bradfute et al., 2024). The virus has a tri-segmented negative- sense single-stranded RNA genome consisting of small, medium, and large segments (Riquelme, 2021). This segmented genome is crucial for facilitating genetic reassortment, thereby aiding the evolution of the virus and the emergence of novel variants (Kim et al., 2021). The small segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein, which is vital for encapsidating RNA, stabilizing the genome, and regulating antiviral signaling in the host (Kell, 2022). Similarly, the large segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase responsible for the transcription and replication of the virus (Bradfute et al., 2024). Envelope glycoproteins form tetrameric spikes on the viral envelope and mediate receptor binding and membrane fusion during host-cell entry (Bradfute et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2021). Accordingly, any struc­ tural alterations in these glycoproteins can affect viral infectivity, tissue tropism, and host adaptation potential (Bradfute et al., 2024). The nucleocapsid protein safeguards viral RNA and enables ribo­ nucleoprotein complex formation, which is essential for replication (Munir et al., 2021). The nucleocapsid protein also modulates host innate immune pathways by interfering with mechanisms responsible for signaling interferons (Kell, 2022). Once hantaviruses enter mam­ malian host cells, they replicate in the cytoplasm, where viral RNA transcription and translation occur using host ribosomes and viral polymerase complexes (Munir et al., 2021). The newly synthesized virions assemble within the Golgi apparatus before they are released via exocytosis (Koehler et al., 2022). To gain entry into host cells, hantaviruses utilize β3 integrins and other endothelial receptors, and they have high tropism for vascular endothelial cells, resulting in cap­ illary leakage, pulmonary edema, and injury to renal vessels (Koehler et al., 2022; Munir et al., 2021). These viruses evade the host immune system by suppressing innate antiviral signaling and interfering with interferon production. However, in the case of rodent reservoirs, per­ sistent infection often results from immune modulation, which limits excessive inflammatory responses, thereby permitting the persistence of the virus (Kell, 2022). 3 Rodent reservoir ecology and viral persistence Rodents have been identified as natural reservoirs for hantavi­ ruses, with distinct viral species linked with rodents through long- term adaptation (Cabrera et al., 2023). In fact, this co-divergence between the causative virus and its reservoir host has contributed to the genetic stability and ecological persistence of the virus across diverse geographic ecosystems (Milholland et al., 2019). As reservoir rodents tend to remain asymptomatic despite chronic infection, there is sustained viral circulation without any detectable mortality in these hosts (Zuo et al., 2021). The virus can establish persistent infection in rodents by modulating innate and adaptive immune responses, thereby avoiding excessive inflammatory damage (Kell, 2022). This alters interferon signaling and enhances immunoregulatory cytokine activity, contributing to the persistence of the virus in in rodent hosts (LaPointe et al., 2023). At the same time, persistent infection is also aided by viral adaptation to host cellular pathways that reduce apop­ tosis and sustain long-term replication (Zhang et al., 2021). However, the pattern and duration of viral shedding from infected rodents remain highly variable depending on the hantavirus host system and stage of infection (Bagamian et al., 2012; Hardestam et al., 2008). A study on bank voles infected with Puumala hantavirus reported the detection of viral RNA in saliva, urine, and feces during defined peri­ ods of infection (Hardestam et al., 2008). Evidence obtained from naturally infected deer mice maintained in outdoor enclosures sug­ gested that indirect environmental transmission may be less efficient than previously assumed (Bagamian et al., 2012). Aerosolization of contaminated rodent excreta is the primary route of transmission of the causative virus to humans, particularly in enclosed settings (Vial et al., 2023). The intensity of virus shedding varies with rodent age, infection stage, season, and ecological factors, Shrivastava et al.  10.3389/fmicb.2026.1943856 Frontiers in Microbiology 03 frontiersin.org as these factors determine the efficiency of viral dissemination (Bagamian et al., 2012; Douglas et al., 2022; Hardestam et al., 2008). Seasonal breeding enhances the number of juvenile rodents that are susceptible to infection, which expedites the process of recurrent amplification of hantavirus transmission, particularly in peak hours (Goodfellow et al., 2021). The ecological dynamics of rodent popula­ tions are affected by rainfall, vegetation growth, and availability of food resources (Chen et al., 2021). Climatic conditions that increase food availability can eventually trigger surges in rodent populations, which further increase viral circulation in reservoir communities (Tian and Stenseth, 2019). In fact, extreme climate events such as El Niño can alter the breeding cycle of rodents and indirectly increase the risk of outbreaks by aiding in the rapid expansion of the rodent reservoir (Ashique et al., 2022). Similarly, an increase in rodent density can facilitate the transmis­ sion of hantavirus through aggressive interactions, biting habits, and close contact with other hosts (Chen et al., 2021). Moreover, juvenile dispersal and territorial overlap play a vital role in sustaining the endemic transmission of the virus (Juan et al., 2019). It is important to note that, despite a reported decline in biodiversity, there is a rise in the dominance of efficient reservoir species, primarily due to reduced ecological competition and regulation by predators (Sánchez et al., 2021). In situations where simplified ecosystems are present, there is an increase in rodent–human interactions and a higher oppor­ tunity for zoonotic spillover (Plowright et al., 2021). Finally, habitat fragmentation and anthropogenic changes in the environment can selectively improve the survival of rodent species that are competent to sustain hantavirus infection circulation (Camp et al., 2021). 4 Climate change as a driver of hantavirus emergence Climate change has been acknowledged as one of the key deter­ minants for hantavirus outbreaks in different parts of the world (Ashique et al., 2022; Douglas et al., 2022; Ecke et al., 2022; Guterres and de Lemos, 2018; Karbalaei et al., 2022; Kell, 2022; Koehler et al., 2022; Moirano et al., 2024; Park et al., 2021; Prist et al., 2021; Tariq and Kim, 2022; Warner et al., 2021). Rising global temperatures due to the greenhouse effect have affected the reproductive cycles, survival rates, and population density of rodents, creating more opportunities for hantavirus amplification within reservoir hosts (Douglas et al., 2022). Similarly, altered precipitation patterns, especially increased rainfall following periods of drought, have resulted in an increase in vegeta­ tion growth and food availability, thereby indirectly promoting the expansion of rodent populations (Ecke et al., 2022). Environmental stressors, such as drought, can change rodent foraging behaviors and their proximity to human habitats, which may increase the potential for human–wildlife contact (Ashique et al., 2022). On the contrary, during floods, rodent populations are displaced from their natural habitats into peri-domestic settings, which then become the source of human–rodent interactions (Douglas et al., 2022). Climate-driven habitat degradation and deforestation activities have also forced reservoir rodents to migrate into agricultural and urbanized areas, as highlighted in a systematic review (Moirano et al., 2024). Similarly, the expansion of peri-urban ecosystems has aided the formation of an ecological interface at which infected rodents can coexist with human populations (Douglas et al., 2022). Moreover, land-use changes by humans coupled with climate stress may alter rodent movement patterns and habitat overlap, potentially creating conditions that facilitate the spillover of infection from rodents to humans (Kell, 2022; Moirano et al., 2024). While environmental tem­ perature and humidity are hypothesized to influence hantavirus per­ sistence outside rodent hosts, the exact duration of infectivity in peri-domestic settings remains a subject of ongoing investigation (Guterres and de Lemos, 2018). In fact, cool and humid conditions tend to prolong the persistence of the virus in rodent excreta, thereby increasing the likelihood of aerosol-mediated transmission of infec­ tion (Koehler et al., 2022). Simultaneously, climate stress can modify the replication dynamics of the causative virus in rodents, which even­ tually alters shedding patterns and transmission intensity (Bagamian et al., 2012; Kell, 2022). Warm climate conditions have played a vital role in the expansion of rodent reservoirs into previously unsuitable ecological regions and higher altitudes (Camp et al., 2021). This redistribution of rodents could potentially increase exposure risks among immunologically naïve human populations (Karbalaei et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). Andes virus outbreaks in South America have been linked to climatic conditions, where ecological alterations and habitat shifts may influ­ ence the overall transmission dynamics (Douglas et al., 2022; Prist et al., 2021). Molecular studies have suggested that ecological attributes might influence the evolution and endemicity of Andes virus in these areas (Warner et al., 2021). Similarly, for Sin Nombre virus (the most common agent of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in humans), climatic attributes, such as increased precipitation and vegetation growth, have been positively linked to periodic increases in deer mouse populations (Goodfellow et al., 2021). Climate change has also influ­ enced rat population dynamics in Europe and East Asia and altered seasonal transmission cycles (Park et al., 2021; Tariq and Kim, 2022). These observations are consistent with current evidence suggest­ ing that climate change affects the transmission of hantavirus through multiple interconnected biological pathways rather than a single envi­ ronmental factor (Ramos-Nino et al., 2026). In other words, tempera­ ture, precipitation, habitat fragmentation, and altered food availability cumulatively alter rodent population dynamics, viral shedding, and opportunities for human exposure (Kumar and John, 2026). However, the reported magnitude of these effects varies across geographical regions, likely due to differences in reservoir specie…

Climate change, rodent ecology, and the rising risk of hantavirus outbreaks: an alarming public health concern Saurabh RamBihariLal Shrivastava 1,2*, Prateek Sudhakar Bobhate 3, Harshal Mendhe 1, Nandkishor Bankar 4, Ashwini Tidake 4 and Prithvi Petkar 1 1Department of Community Medicine, Datta Meghe Medical College, Datta Meghe Institute of Higher Education and Research, Nagpur, Maharashtra, India, 2Dr. D. Y. Patil School of Allied Health Sciences, Dr. D. Y. Patil Vidyapeeth, Pune (Deemed to be University), Pimpri, Pune, Maharashtra, India, 3Department of Community Medicine, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Vijaypur, Jammu, India, 4Department of Microbiology, Datta Meghe Medical College, Datta Meghe Institute of Higher Education and Research, Nagpur, Maharashtra, India The Anthropocene era has been characterized by a higher risk of zoonotic viral outbreaks, which often result from a combination of factors, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, land-use patterns, and increased opportunities for human–animal interactions. The current perspective provides an integrated synthesis of how climate change-driven alterations in rodent ecology impact the molecular evolution, transmission dynamics, and emergence of hantaviruses, with an emphasis on the underlying virological mechanisms and their implica­ tions for One Health preparedness. Hantaviruses have undergone extensive diversification throughout their evolution and host adaptation and can infect rodents, bats, reptiles, and fish. Rodents serve as the principal natural reservoirs for hantaviruses, with many viral species exhibiting long-term evolutionary asso­ ciations with specific rodent host species. Climate change has been recognized as one of the key determinants for the emergence of hantavirus outbreaks in dif­ ferent parts of the world. Climate-related factors may facilitate viral amplification through multiple mechanisms, including their impact on evolution, mutation, and reassortment. To conclude, climate change has shaped the ecology, transmission dynamics, and molecular evolution of hantaviruses by altering rodent behav­ ior, their habitats, and the environmental persistence of viral particles. Climate- induced ecological disruption has created opportunities for viral amplification within reservoir hosts and augmented the risk of zoonotic spillover into humans. These insights provide a conceptual framework for anticipating future outbreaks in the context of climate change and support the integration of ecological, viro­ logical, and public health surveillance systems. There is an urgent need to ensure that virological preparedness strategies evolve in accordance with changing envi­ ronmental conditions by strengthening genomic surveillance and integrated One Health frameworks. A rise in the probability of the emergence of infectious diseases with epi­ demic or pandemic potential has been reported in the last few decades due to environmental disruption, which has increased spillover from wildlife reservoirs to human populations (Plowright et al., 2021). With increasing climate-sensitive viral outbreaks, there is a crucial need to understand the ecological determinants of virus transmission and the necessity to adopt integrated One Health surveillance frameworks (Stephens et al., 2021). In fact, artificial intelligence-based predictive models have estimated that climate-induced shifts in wildlife distribu­ tion can facilitate novel cross-species viral transmission in the future (Grange et al., 2021). Among zoonotic pathogens, hantaviruses have attracted signifi­ cant scientific attention because they are highly adaptable rodent- borne RNA viruses capable of causing severe diseases, namely, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmo­ nary syndrome, in humans (Munir et al., 2021). Moreover, changing climatic conditions, such as varying rainfall patterns, warmer tem­ peratures, and ecological instability, can influence fluctuations in res­ ervoir populations of rodents and create more opportunities for hantavirus transmission to humans (Vial et al., 2023). Recent studies and developments have improved our understanding of the ecology of the causative viruses, environmental determinants, and surveillance approaches (Munir et al., 2021; Ramos-Nino et al., 2026; Vial et al., 2023). However, the majority of studies have focused on exploring climate variability, rodent population dynamics, viral evolution, and public health preparedness as separate domains (Fabbri et al., 2025; Grange et al., 2021; Munir et al., 2021; Ramos-Nino et al., 2026; Stephens et al., 2021; Vial et al., 2023). The current perspective pro­ vides an integrated synthesis of how climate change-driven alterations in rodent ecology impact the molecular evolution, transmission dynamics, and emergence of hantaviruses, highlighting the underlying virological mechanisms and their implications for One Health preparedness. 2 Hantaviruses: virological and molecular overview Hantaviruses belong to the family Hantaviridae (order Bunyavirales), which includes multiple genera and several species, the majority of which are pathogenic to humans (Kuhn and Schmaljohn, 2023). These viruses have shown extensive diversification in their evo­ lution and host adaptation as they can infect rodents, bats, reptiles, and fish (Bradfute et al., 2024). The virus has a tri-segmented negative- sense single-stranded RNA genome consisting of small, medium, and large segments (Riquelme, 2021). This segmented genome is crucial for facilitating genetic reassortment, thereby aiding the evolution of the virus and the emergence of novel variants (Kim et al., 2021). The small segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein, which is vital for encapsidating RNA, stabilizing the genome, and regulating antiviral signaling in the host (Kell, 2022). Similarly, the large segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase responsible for the transcription and replication of the virus (Bradfute et al., 2024). papers.title: Hantavirus infections: A growing global health concern
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are increasingly regarded as an important emerging risk to global health, with an estimated annual impact on more than 200000 people worldwide. These pathogens are single-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the family Han taviridae and are known to cause two major clinical syndromes in humans: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS). The so-called old world hantaviruses, which are associated with HFRS, are predominantly distributed across Asia, Europe, and parts of Africa. In contrast, new world hantaviruses, responsible for HPS, are largely confined to North and South America. Each year, approximately 150000-200000 HFRS cases require hospitalization globally, with the greatest burden occurring in developing regions. The mortality rate of HFRS ranges from below 1% to about 12%, depending on the infecting strain. Both disease forms are characterized by increased capillary permeability, leading to clinical features such as hypotension, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis. While HFRS has a broader geographic distribution, HPS carries a higher risk of death.. Moreover, the detection of new viral strains and the steady rise in reported cases have intensified global concern. Enhancing surveillance systems and expanding laboratory diagnostic capacity are therefore essential for effective monitoring and control of hantavirus diseases.

papers.full_text: Andes virus from the 2026 MV Hondius outbreak does not show enhanced entry into human cells The recent outbreak of Andes orthohantavirus (Andes virus, ANDV) aboard the MV Hondius has thus far resulted in 13 confirmed cases, including three fatalities, and has rapidly evolved into an international health crisis. ANDV is a zoonotic New World hantavirus whose main reservoir is the long-tailed colilargo, and that causes severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in humans. Transmission to humans usually occurs through contact with aerosols from secretions or excretions of infected rodents. Although several seasonal outbreaks occur regularly, mainly in Chile and Argentina, transmission chains are usually short-lived and involve limited person-to-person transmission. Nevertheless, the recent outbreak is thought to have involved up to three generation transmission chains. Sequenced isolates from the MV Hondius outbreak harbour several nonsynonymous mutations throughout their genomes compared to reference strains and isolates from previous outbreaks, while exhibiting little genetic divergence within the 2026 outbreak cluster. Such nonsynonymous mutations include two changes in the RdRp, one change in the N protein, and six changes affecting the glycoprotein complex (GPC) (Supplementary Table 1). Whether these sequence polymorphisms enhance ANDV capacity to infect human cells remains unknown. Andes virus surface glycoproteins associated with different outbreaks exhibit similar entry into human cells. (A) Phylogenetic analysis of M segments of Andes virus strains isolated in humans. Sixty nucleotide sequences corresponding to >90% complete M segments of ANDV isolates sampled from humans were retrieved from Pathoplexus and aligned with MAFFT. Phylogenetic reconstruction was performed using the TIM2 + F + G4 substitution model. Accession numbers are indicated at branch tips for each sequence. Sin Nombre virus was used as outgroup. Scale bar: 0.10 changes per site. (B) Schematics of surface glycoproteins from CHI-7913, Epuyen/2018 and SWITZ/2026 isolates. Non-synonymous changes compared to the CHI-7913 sequence are depicted by black lines, and specific amino acid changes are indicated below. GC ectodomain and GN head and base domains are indicated with coloured boxes. (C) VSV pseudotypes were titrated on the indicated cell lines. Data show the correlation between viral titres of SWITZ/2026 strain and CHI-7913 (left) or Epuyen/2018 (right), in infectious units per volume unit (IU/mL). Each dot corresponds to the average of n = 3 independent pseudotype production and titration experiments. Error bars show the SEM. The Pearson correlation r and best-fit values ± 95% confidence intervals for a simple linear regression are shown. (D) Incorporation of ANDV surface glycoproteins in VSV particles was assessed via Western Blot and quantified as the GPC/VSV-M ratio. (E) Lentiviral particles bearing each ANDV glycoprotein were titrated on the indicated cell lines. Bars are set at the mean. Each dot corresponds to an independent pseudotype production and titration experiment (n = 3). Statistical significance was assessed on log-transformed titres with a 2-way ANOVA with repeated measures considering each independent production and infection block as the matching factor and Tukey’s post-hoc test for multiple comparisons. Five visuals: one phylogenetic tree, one protein domain diagram, two scatter plots, one Western blot, and one bar chart comparing Andes virus data. The figure shows five visuals comparing Andes virus glycoproteins from CHI-7913, Epuyen/2018, and SWITZ/2026. A phylogenetic tree on the left arranges Andes virus M segment sequences from Argentina, Chile, Switzerland, and Brazil, with Sin Nombre virus as the outgroup. Branches terminate in isolate names and years, and colored markers indicate bootstrap support from 0 to 100 on a horizontal color scale bar. A protein domain diagram at top right displays glycoprotein layouts for CHI-7913, Epuyen/2018, and SWITZ/2026 along a horizontal position axis labeled amino acid, from 0 to about 1100. Rectangles mark GN head, GN base, and GC ectodomain, with mutations marked by vertical ticks and labels. Two scatter plots labeled vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) pseudotypes plot SWITZ/2026 titer on the vertical axis versus CHI-7913 or Epuyen/2018 titer on the horizontal axis, both axes labeled log base 10 infectious units per milliliter, spanning about 4 to 8 with ticks at intervals of 1. Colored points mark individual human cell lines, regression lines follow a diagonal trend, and insets report r equals 0.99, slope near 1.00, and y intercept near 0.0. A Western blot below shows His-Tag and VSV-M bands for empty, CHI-7913, Epuyen/2018, and SWITZ/2026 lanes, with a GPC over VSV-M ratio reported as 0.45, 0.45, and 0.48. A grouped bar chart labeled lentiviruses plots titer on the vertical axis, log base 10 infectious units per milliliter from 3 to about 6, across HEK-293T, Huh-7, A549, SNB-19, ADR-RES, CAKI-1, and HUVEC cell lines, comparing CHI-7913, Epuyen/2018, and SWITZ/2026 bars; statistical markers labeled ns appear above bars. Entry of hantaviruses into host cells is mediated by GPC, encoded in the M segment. We sought to assess the capacity of the GPC from an MV Hondius isolate (SWITZ/2026) to mediate entry into human cells and to compare its entry efficiency with those of a reference human strain (CHI-7913) and an isolate from a previous human outbreak in Argentina in 2018 (Epuyen/2018) (Figure 1(A)). Relative to CHI-7913, the Epuyen/2018 and SWITZ/2026 isolates each harbour six nonsynonymous amino acid substitutions in their GPC, both sharing only one substitution (I11 V, Figure 1(B)). To focus solely on viral entry, we generated single-cycle vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) pseudotypes bearing the three ANDV GPCs. We then compared their infectivity across a panel of nine human cell lines, selected because they express known ANDV receptors (PCDH1: 0.1-13.3 fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads [FPKMs], Integrin Subunit Alpha V: 0.9-6.2 FPKMs, Integrin Subunit Beta 3: 0.0-1.5 FPKMs) and because we previously demonstrated their susceptibility to the entry of other New World hantaviruses. Additionally, we included Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) as a relevant primary endothelial cell model for ANDV infection. Viral titres spanned two orders of magnitude across all nine cell lines, with Huh-7 and ADR-RES cells exhibiting the highest and lowest susceptibility, respectively (Figure 1(C)). Titres of SWITZ/2026-GPC pseudotypes showed a strong positive correlation with those of CHI-7913 and Epuyen/2018 (r = 0.99 in both cases). Simple linear regression yielded slopes of 1.00 ± 0.04 (95% CI) and 0.95 ± 0.03 for CHI-7913 and Epuyen/2018, respectively, while estimates for the Y-intercept were 0.04 ± 0.25 (CHI-7913) and 0.38 ± 0.16 (Epuyen/2018). Taken together, these results indicate that the infectivity of SWITZ/2026 pseudotypes does not differ significantly from that of either CHI-7913 or Epuyen/2018 pseudotypes. Western blot analysis confirmed comparable incorporation of all three GPCs into VSV particles (Figure 1(D)). Finally, to rule out any potential confounding effects associated with the VSV backbone, we generated lentiviral pseudotypes bearing each ANDV GPC and similarly titrated them in human cell lines. Titres of SWITZ/2026 lentiviral pseudotypes did not differ significantly from those of CHI-7913 or Epuyen/2018 in any of the cell lines tested, further corroborating the findings described above (Figure 1(E)). Collectively, our results suggest that the GPC of the ANDV strain isolated aboard the MV Hondius mediates entry into human cells as efficiently as that of previous isolates, arguing against enhanced viral entry as the main determinant of the outbreak. The observed transmission dynamics may instead reflect the confined, high-contact environment aboard the cruise ship, similar to what was reported during the Epuyén outbreak. However, contributions from genetic variation in viral segments other than M, potentially affecting genome replication or other aspects of viral biology such as immune escape, tissue tropism, or viral shedding, cannot be excluded. Supplementary Material Supplemental Material Supplemental data for this article can be accessed online at https://doi.org/10.1080/22221751.2026.2732719. References The evolution and emergence of hantaviruses A global perspective on hantavirus ecology, epidemiology, and disease Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak in Argentina: molecular evidence for person-to-person transmission of Andes virus Person-to-person household and nosocomial transmission of Andes hantavirus, Southern Chile, 2011 Andes hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship, 2026 . Virological. 2026; published online May 10; [cited 2026 Jun 9]. Available from: https://virological.org/t/preliminary-analysis-of-orthohantavirus-andesense-virus-sequences-from-a-cruise-ship-related-cluster-may-2026/1029 Andes virus recognition of human and Syrian hamster beta3 integrins is determined by an L33P substitution in the PSI domain Protocadherin-1 is essential for cell entry by new world hantaviruses Receptor-binding proteins from animal viruses are broadly compatible with human cell entry factors “Super-Spreaders” and person-to-person transmission of Andes virus in Argentina

analysis.background: The 2026 outbreak of Andes orthohantavirus (ANDV) aboard the MV Hondius caused 13 confirmed human cases, including three deaths, raising concerns about potential changes in viral transmissibility (F1).
analysis.methods: Sequenced isolates from the outbreak were compared to reference strains (F6) and phylogenetic analysis of >90% complete M‑segment sequences was performed using MAFFT alignment and a TIM2+F+G4 model (F11‑F13). Entry potential was assessed with VSV pseudotypes bearing each isolate’s glycoproteins on several human cell lines, titrated in triplicate (n = 3) and correlated by linear regression (F19‑F23). Incorporation of glycoproteins into VSV particles was examined by Western blot (F24), and lentiviral particles bearing the same glycoproteins were titrated on the same cell lines with 2‑way ANOVA (F25‑F28).
analysis.results: ANDV glycoproteins from the 2026 SWITZ/2026 strain showed entry efficiencies comparable to earlier CHI‑7913 and Epuyen/2018 strains (F9), with VSV pseudotype titres highly correlated (Pearson r = 0.99, slope ≈ 1.0) (F20‑F23, F36) and no significant differences in lentiviral titres (F26). Western blot indicated similar GPC/VSV‑M ratios across strains (F24).
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates that the recent outbreak isolates do not possess enhanced capacity to infect human cells, informing surveillance and risk‑assessment frameworks for ANDV transmission (F9, F19‑F23, F25‑F28).
analysis.limitations: Entry assays were limited to in‑vitro pseudotype systems on a few human cell lines with small replicate numbers (n = 3) (F21) and statistical analysis was confined to log‑transformed titres; broader in‑vivo or clinical correlates were not examined (F28).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The 2026 MV Hondius outbreak of Andes virus caused 13 confirmed cases and three deaths, prompting investigation of viral transmissibility (F1). Methods: Outbreak isolates were sequenced, phylogenetically analyzed, and their glycoproteins tested in VSV pseudotype and lentiviral entry assays on human cell lines (n = 3), with Western blot and statistical analyses (F6, F11‑F13, F19‑F28). Results: Glycoproteins from the 2026 strain entered human cells as efficiently as earlier strains, showing a Pearson r = 0.99 correlation and no significant titre differences (F9, F20‑F23, F26, F36). Contribution: Findings indicate the recent isolates lack enhanced human cell entry, aiding surveillance and risk assessment (F9, F19‑F23, F25‑F28). Limitations: Experiments were limited to in‑vitro assays on few cell lines with small replicate numbers and lack in‑vivo validation (F21, F28).

analysis_zh.results: 2026年SWITZ/2026株的安第斯病毒糖蛋白显示进入效率与早期CHI-7913和Epuyen/2018株相当(F9),VSV伪型病毒滴度高度相关(Pearson r = 0.99,斜率≈1.0)(F20–F23,F36),慢病毒滴度无显著差异(F26)。Western blot显示各株间GPC/VSV-M比例相似(F24)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究表明,近期疫情分离株并未具备增强感染人类细胞的能力,为安第斯病毒传播的监测与风险评估框架提供信息(F9,F19–F23,F25–F28)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 进入实验仅限于少数人类细胞系的体外伪型系统,复制次数少(n=3)(F21),统计分析仅限于对数转换滴度;未检验更广泛的体内或临床相关性(F28)。

papers.title: Multi-omics Reveals Divergent Endothelial Molecular Responses to New and Old World Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes that vary in clinical manifestation and severity. Although tissue tropism contributes to these differences, both Old and New World hantaviruses infect endothelial cells, where species-specific disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Here we integrated time-resolved global RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics of human endothelial cells infected with New World Andes virus (ANDV) or Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV). Despite equivalent early viral RNA and protein levels, ANDV elicited a stronger innate immune protein response, preceding its restriction while HTNV replication continued. At later stages of infection, HTNV induced downregulation of cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation, accompanied by visual disruption of cellular actin architecture. Additionally, ANDV induced heightened activity of ERBB-family kinases, whose chemical inhibition by neratinib and afatinib reduced viral replication. Together, these data define species-specific responses in endothelial cells, identify druggable host targets, and reveal mechanisms with relevance to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes with variable severity. Methods: Time‑resolved RNA‑seq, proteomics, and phosphoproteomics were applied to human endothelial cells infected with Andes virus or Hantaan virus. papers.title_zh: 多组学揭示新世界和旧世界汉坦病毒的内皮分子反应差异

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 引起血管渗漏综合征,临床表现和严重程度各异。
analysis_zh.methods: 对感染新世界安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)或旧世界汉滩病毒(汉滩病毒)的人类内皮细胞进行综合时间分辨全局RNA测序、质谱蛋白质组学和磷酸蛋白质组学分析。
analysis_zh.results: 尽管早期病毒RNA和蛋白水平相当,安第斯病毒诱导更强的先天免疫蛋白响应并先于其受限出现,而汉滩病毒复制持续进行;随后,汉滩病毒导致细胞骨架和连接蛋白磷酸化下调,并伴随肌动蛋白结构的可视化破坏;安第斯病毒引起ERBB家族激酶活性升高,使用neratinib或afatinib进行化学抑制可降低病毒复制。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该数据定义了物种特异性内皮反应,识别出可药物化宿主靶点,并揭示了与不同血管渗漏症状学相关的机制。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;未报告详细方法、样本量、统计分析以及体内验证。

papers.title: Hantavirus Across Travel, Climate, and Clinical Frontiers: A Global Scoping Review of Emerging Risks (1978-2026)
papers.abstract: This scoping review aims to map the available literature on emerging hantavirus risks across three frontiers: travel-related exposure, climatic and environmental drivers, and clinical frontiers (diagnosis, misdiagnosis, and underrecognition). Following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, the review will systematically search thirteen databases and platforms for literature published between 1978 and 2026. Ultimately, this research will map the global evidence landscape, identify knowledge gaps, and highlight priorities for surveillance, travel medicine, climate adaptation, and clinical education.

papers.full_text: Letters to the Editor 1 Research Letter Hantavirus Infection as a Mimic of Rheumatic Disease: A Selective Diagnostic Approach To the Editor: Recent public health alerts have renewed attention to hantavirus infection, an uncommon but potentially severe zoonosis.1,2 For rheumatologists, its relevance is selective but clinically important in compatible contexts. Hantavirus infection may initially present as an acute febrile inflammatory syndrome with arthritis, arthralgia, or myalgia, variably accompanied by thrombocytopenia, endothelial dysfunction, and renal or pulmonary involvement.3 In patients referred for suspected rheumatic disease, this constellation of signs and symptoms may overlap with inflammatory arthritis, systemic autoimmune disease, immune-mediated renal disease, or vasculitis. The central issue is a diagnostic one: Hantavirus may behave as an infectious mimic of rheumatic disease while the diagnostic evaluation is still ongoing, and treatment decisions may have substantial consequences. Hantavirus should not be considered on the basis of isolated fever or musculoskeletal symptoms alone. Rather, it should enter the rheumatology differential when fever and musculoskeletal manifestations occur together with thrombocytopenia and renal, urinary, pulmonary, capillary leak, or hemorrhagic features, especially when epidemiologic exposure is compatible. Clinically, this phenotype may resemble selected rheumatic presentations, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)–associated vasculitis, antiglomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease, adult-onset Still disease, inflammatory myopathy, infection-triggered arthritis, or undifferentiated systemic autoimmune disease. Relevant exposures include contact with rodents or rodent-contaminated environments, occupational or domestic exposure in rural or peridomestic settings, recent travel to endemic areas, or exposure associated with an epidemiologically linked hantavirus cluster.3 The epidemiologic pattern is geographically structured. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is encountered mainly across Europe and Asia, whereas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is recognized chiefly in the Americas, with the distribution of individual orthohantaviruses determined by the ecology of their reservoir hosts.3 To date, limited ­ person-to-person transmission has been documented only for Andes virus, a hantavirus endemic to South America.3 The published literature, although limited, illustrates several diagnostic challenges relevant to rheumatology. Musculoskeletal involvement is usually nonspecific; arthralgia and myalgia may accompany HFRS and, in some adults, may be sufficiently prominent to resemble an early inflammatory presentation.4 Thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, proteinuria, hema- turia, and hypocomplementemia may prompt consideration of systemic autoimmune or immune-mediated renal disease, including SLE, vasculitis, immune-mediated nephritis, and anti-GBM disease, thereby increasing the risk of diagnostic misclassification. Hantavirus-induced acute kidney injury may mimic immune-mediated glomerular disease, including anti-GBM disease or lupus nephritis, before serologic confirma- tion clarifies the diagnosis.5,6 Vasculitis-like presentations require particular caution. A recent report described myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA– positive pauci-immune small vessel vasculitis with progressive renal dysfunction during acute hantavirus infection.7 This obser- vation establishes a temporal and clinical association but does not demonstrate causation. Earlier serologic data also argue against a frequent relationship. Among 191 patients with estab- lished systemic vasculitides, including granulomatosis with poly- angiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and giant cell arteritis, no hantavirus-specific antibodies were detected.8 These findings therefore support diag- nostic vigilance rather than a causal interpretation, particularly when infection-related organ injury and primary autoimmune vasculitis share clinical, serological, or histopathological features. SARS-CoV-2 infection may offer a useful clinical reference for rheumatologists when considering the interface between viral infection and rheumatic disease. Both SARS-CoV-2 and hantaviruses are RNA viruses capable of eliciting prominent systemic inflammatory responses and, in selected cases, arthritis or vasculitis-like manifestations that may resemble ­ immune-mediated disease.3,9,10 Experience with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has heightened awareness that viral infections may both mimic and intersect with rheumatic phenotypes. Hantavirus infection may be viewed within this same diagnostic framework, although the underlying biology and clinical syndromes are distinct. From a clinical perspective, severe hantavirus disease, particularly HCPS, may progress rapidly to fulminant cardiopulmonary failure, with case fatality rates reaching up to 50% in the Americas.2,3 Accordingly, hantavirus testing should be guided by the overall clinical and epidemiologic pattern rather than used routinely in rheumatology. Serologic testing may be appropriate when fever and musculoskeletal symptoms coexist with throm- bocytopenia, renal or pulmonary involvement, and a compatible exposure history; reverse transcription PCR can be considered in selected settings according to disease timing, severity, and local laboratory availability. Testing is most useful while the differen- tial diagnosis remains unresolved, particularly before substantial immunomodulatory treatment is initiated. The Figure summa- rizes this selective approach. The central practical implication is selective case recognition rather than routine screening. During periods of increased hanta- virus activity or recognized outbreaks, testing should be reserved for patients in whom the clinical phenotype and exposure history are concordant. Such an approach may reduce premature diagnostic closure, help distinguish infection-related endothelial The Journal of Rheumatology 2026;xx:xxxx doi:10.3899/jrheum.2026-0485 First Release September 15 2026 © 2026 The Journal of Rheumatology 2 The Journal of Rheumatology injury from primary rheumatic disease, and support more accu- rate classification of acute febrile inflammatory presentations. In selected cases, distinguishing infection-related inflammatory presentations, including hantavirus-associated disease, from primary rheumatic disease may also affect the timing or appro- priateness of immunomodulatory therapy.
